talks.title: ICS4ICS
talks.teaser: Details ICS4ICS and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
The talk gives an update on ICS for ICS, a volunteer effort to adapt the FEMA Incident Command System to cyber incidents, especially those affecting industrial control systems. The speaker, who has an emergency management background, argues that cyber responses lack a shared framework, which makes them hard to scale, drains responders, and leaves organizations with incompatible playbooks and terminology. She notes that cyber is the only federally recognized disaster type not formally using the system, and presents its structure of common terms, clear roles, manageable span of control and a planning cycle as a fix for failures seen in past major catastrophes.

The speaker then reviews progress over the past two years: about 1,000 global volunteers, a first group of cyber incident commanders credentialed through FEMA's One Responder system, and work on training, outreach and exercise materials. A recent exercise simulated a type 3, single-company incident in which an HVAC malfunction had to be investigated for both an equipment fault and a cyber cause at the same time. Participants praised the all-hazards approach, the standard FEMA forms and the structured decision-making. Their improvement points were to brief people on the forms beforehand, to make clear that the incident commander has final authority, and to give smaller companies guidance on adopting the structure.

Looking ahead, the program plans more exercises, customized forms, wider credentialing and mutual-aid templates. Practitioners are invited to take the free FEMA courses, join the volunteer team, host or observe exercises, or present on the topic. The main takeaway is that cyber responders can borrow proven emergency management practices rather than invent new ones, and that organizations should run the full planning cycle instead of jumping from planning straight to exercising.

talks.title: Zero Trust Applications For The Grid
talks.teaser: Discusses zero Trust Applications For The Grid and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at applying zero trust principles to electric grid equipment. The speaker walks through a microgrid test site in North Carolina that runs islanded most of the time and hosts distributed control applications. Early work found that substation devices had no cryptographic identity and that their traffic traveled in clear text. A 2015 demonstration on a substation mock-up showed how easily network traffic could be observed, and how an ARP spoof could take over a controller and send commands to protection relays.

To close those gaps, the team overlays a Kubernetes cluster on industrial PCs at the site. Adapters hide legacy Modbus and DNP3 devices behind a translation layer that publishes harmonized data over a message bus. Each workload gets an identity and certificate from a SPIFFE-based server, with an intermediate certificate authority inside the microgrid, so workloads communicate over mutual TLS. Certificates can be refreshed on a schedule, and the local server is refreshed from a higher level. The last link to field devices is still handled with a bump-in-the-wire device, and MACsec is discussed as a possible option.

The speaker closes with open problems: recovering after a long outage when certificates expire, authenticating field endpoints, and getting protection engineers to accept added latency. The main takeaway is that identity and encryption should move into edge devices, and that interoperable designs need outside review and attempts to break them.

talks.title: SUNBURST From The Inside
talks.teaser: Discusses SUNBURST From The Inside - Tim Brown, CISO of SolarWinds and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
This talk looks at the SolarWinds build-system compromise from the response side rather than the technical side. The speaker, the company's CISO, describes the first days after a call from the CEO in December 2020 reporting that a security firm had found tainted code. He explains that the attackers had been doing email reconnaissance since late 2019, ran a no-op test insertion in November, and then placed code into the build environment between March and June, bypassing source control. Three product versions were affected, and about 18,000 customers had downloaded one of them.

The middle of the talk covers how the team organized. Engineering, IT, business escalation, customer outreach and communications each had a lead, and an outside legal firm acted as coordinator. Forensic teams from CrowdStrike and KPMG searched for evidence, and the team worked with the FBI and CISA. The company issued a 10-K within about a day and a half, handled a support queue that reached roughly 19,000 tickets, revoked its code-signing certificate, rebuilt and reshipped its products, and moved to build pipelines that compare outputs before release.

The speaker's takeaways are that a standard incident response program is not enough at this scale. He recommends choosing partners who can escalate quickly, expecting to be outnumbered and misreported, ignoring press noise while staying focused on customers, being open about what is known, and building executive communication skills before a crisis.

talks.title: Navigating International Law In Critical Infrastructure Cyber Events
talks.teaser: Demonstrates navigating International Law In Critical Infrastructure Cyber Events and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
### Overview
This panel session from the S4 conference, moderated by Maggie (Product Security Research Manager at Rockwell Automation), explores the complex challenges of applying international humanitarian law (IHL) and the law of armed conflict (LOAC) to cyber events targeting critical infrastructure and operational technology (OT). Featuring Joe Slowik (Gigamon and Paralus) and Danielle Jablanski (Nozomi Networks and Atlantic Council), the discussion examines foundational international law principles—distinction, proportionality, necessity, and self-defense—and interrogates how they intersect with modern cyber network operations, offensive tooling, and state proxy behaviors.

### Key Topics
- **Dual-Use Tension (Espionage vs. Destructive Action):** Initial reconnaissance, access development, and deployment techniques for cyber espionage often look identical to preparations for kinetic or disruptive attacks. Highlighting examples like Nobelium/SolarWinds, Ukrainian wipers, Dragonfly, and Palmetto Fusion, the panelists discuss the difficulty of determining when an operation transitions from intelligence collection into a military armed conflict action, noting that threat actor attribution becomes critical for discerning mission and intent.
- **Defining Combatants and Accountability in Cyberspace:** Traditional LOAC definitions rely on uniformed combatants belonging to state armed forces. Cyberspace complicates this with fluid roles across development teams, access brokers, effects teams, contractors, and cybercriminal syndicates. The panel debates whether developers (e.g., Chernovite regarding Incontroller/Pipedream, or commercial defense contractors) bear legal or retaliatory responsibility compared to deployment teams, citing the US Treasury OFAC sanctions against TsNIIKhM (associated with Xenotime and Triton). Danielle highlights that combatant status in practice shifts toward what entities target and the societal impacts of those actions.
- **Arms Control and Due Care for Cyber Capabilities:** Applying traditional arms control regimes (e.g., Wassenaar) to cyber capabilities faces immense hurdles. The panel addresses commercial dual-use software (such as Cobalt Strike), code leaks, public virus repositories (e.g., VirusTotal hosting Triton framework artifacts), and the responsibilities of security firms and researchers. Technical constraints within payloads—such as Incontroller and Industroyer2's hardcoded configurations or Stuxnet's narrow targeting—are evaluated alongside the reality that enabling mechanisms and zero-days frequently spread far beyond intended targets.
- **Rules of Engagement and Impact Thresholds:** The speakers contrast the formal doctrine of entities like US Cyber Command (e.g., Defend Forward) with the opaque operational thresholds of adversarial agencies like the SVR or GRU, as well as cybercriminal groups like Conti that walk back state-alignment declarations out of self-interest. Danielle and Joe note that unlike nuclear doctrine, cyber conflict lacks clear, agreed-upon fallout impact thresholds to define when an event constitutes an armed attack or cyber warfare.

### Technical Details
- **Malware & Campaigns Referenced:** Triton/Xenotime (targeting safety controllers/SIS), Stuxnet (targeting Siemens Step 7 PLCs and centrifuges), Industroyer2 (noted for hardcoded configuration parameters), Incontroller/Pipedream (associated with the Chernovite group), Cobalt Strike, Nobelium (SolarWinds supply chain event), Dragonfly, Palmetto Fusion, and recent Ukrainian wipers and NotPetya-style supply-chain backdoors.
- **Accidental Disruption in OT:** Fragile industrial control systems and PLCs can suffer unintended disruption from benign or espionage activities (e.g., knocking over a PLC while dumping configurations, or ambiguous cases like the 2014 German steel mill incident).

### Takeaways
- International legal frameworks developed for physical warfare struggle with cyber realities where military targets are blurred with civil society and critical infrastructure.
- The cyber domain still lacks a critical mass of precedent and standardized fallout/impact models to establish definitive thresholds between espionage, crime, and cyber warfare.
- Organizations must focus on potential impact severity and resilience rather than relying solely on adversary intent or traditional legal boundaries.

talks.title: Incident Command System For ICS (ICS4ICS) Exercise at S4x22
talks.teaser: Investigates incident Command System For ICS (ICS4ICS) Exercise at S4x22 and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
This session is a facilitated tabletop exercise from S4x22, run by the ISA Global Cybersecurity Alliance, that shows how the ICS for ICS program manages a significant cyber incident affecting industrial control systems. It combines the Incident Command System, which first responders have used for decades, with computer incident response and the knowledge of industrial control system engineers. The exercise uses a fictional company where a phishing campaign leads to rising office temperatures, malware is confirmed in the HVAC system, and the event is escalated to a CERT director who declares an incident.

The exercise then walks through the planning P cycle. The incident commander sets priorities of life safety, incident stabilization and environmental preservation, and then staffs command and general staff roles such as operations, planning, finance, safety and public information. Each step is supported by standard forms, including the ICS 201 briefing, ICS 202 objectives, ICS 215 operational worksheet and ICS 204 assignment list. In the second operational period the scenario adds repeated false fire alarms, sprinkler water damage and a ransomware payment demand. The team works through a decision process involving the crisis management team, legal counsel and a media inquiry.

The main takeaways are that the framework works best when it is practised before a real event, through tabletop drills, community exercises and the free FEMA online courses. The structure can be scaled down to a type three incident, and even a two-person team can apply its unity of command and clear roles. The organisers also explained that documented decisions help with post-incident review, and they gathered audience feedback and outlined plans for further exercises and credentialing.

talks.title: A Deep Dive Into The DDS Protocol Ta Lun Yen
talks.teaser: Presents A Deep Dive Into The DDS Protocol Ta Lun Yen and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
The talk examines the Data Distribution Service (DDS), a publish-subscribe middleware used in robotics such as ROS 2, autonomous vehicles, trains, aerospace and defense systems. The researchers evaluated six major DDS implementations, found flaws in each of them, and also reported a weakness in the specification itself to the DDS Consortium. They explain why they focused on protocol parsers and XML configuration handling, since both are complex and receive data from untrusted sources.

For fuzzing, they paired a coverage-guided fuzzer with the Unicorn engine so they could test compiled binaries quickly while keeping control of program state. Their campaign against network stack parsers exposed denial-of-service crashes caused by missing input sanitization and weak error handling. Manually altering fields in captured packets, including an IP address field, revealed a reflection issue because the specification does not restrict which addresses may be placed there. They chose the term network reflection attack rather than amplification, since the amplification factor was low. In a separate case, one vendor shipped an outdated XML library with a changed version string, which allowed local code execution, and in configuration-update scenarios that could extend to remote takeover.

An internet scan found roughly 2,300 exposed DDS endpoints, many running outdated versions. The speakers recommend network segmentation and intrusion prevention for systems that cannot be patched, and they stress cooperative vendor engagement. Responses varied: some vendors helped, while others ignored reports or threatened legal action. Most affected vendors have since released fixes.

talks.title: 25 Reasons Information Sharing Fails
talks.teaser: Presents 25 Reasons Information Sharing Fails and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
### Overview
This talk examines historical patterns of information sharing failures across major crises—including Pearl Harbor, September 11, Hurricane Katrina, the Virginia Tech shooting, Deepwater Horizon, and the cyber incident at the Oldsmar water utility. The speaker argues that these catastrophes were not failures of technology, as adequate sensors, radars, and processing tools existed, but failures of people and information architecture. As modern industrial control systems (ICS) and operational technology (OT) transition away from isolated, hierarchical architectures (such as the traditional Purdue model) toward highly connected, cloud-integrated ecosystems, addressing recurring information sharing breakdowns becomes essential to securing critical infrastructure and supply chains.

### Key Topics
- **Recurring Failure Patterns**: Examples include conflation of authority or ambiguity of responsibility (e.g., lower-ranking liaisons at Pearl Harbor; overlapping jurisdictions among the FAA, FBI, and intelligence bodies during 9/11; IT vs. OT responsibility collisions regarding TeamViewer in Oldsmar). Another recurring failure is the lack of verification of critical features or decisions (e.g., misinterpreted war warnings in Hawaii, unverified detainee risks prior to 9/11, untracked FEMA requests in Katrina, and unverified TeamViewer operations in Oldsmar until chemical levels were altered).
- **Shift to Collaborative Outcomes**: Sharing information purely for the sake of sharing typically triggers common failure modes. Information sharing programs must instead be anchored to predefined collaborative outcomes, which dictate necessary data fusion, communication channels, and partnership structures.
- **Case Studies in Operational Collaboration**:
  - *Food Shield*: Developed after a salsa contamination incident was mistakenly blamed on Florida tomatoes rather than Mexican peppers. Food Shield established specific collaborative outcomes, document repositories, and a Common Organizational Registry Environment (CORE), reducing response resolution times from months to 72 hours.
  - *Joint Cyber Defense Collaborative (JCDC)*: An initiative focused on shifting ICS cybersecurity toward operational collaboration, referencing instances such as Microsoft sharing threat intelligence on new malware with the White House and European allies during Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

### Technical Details
- **Digitization & Value Drivers in OT**: Modern systems demand shared architectures due to efficiency and economic value. In South Bend, Indiana, deployment of ~200 flow and level sensors connected to gateways and cloud analytics replaced an estimated $850 million physical overhaul with a $200 million sensor-driven solution. The implementation introduced an automated bidding mechanism for downstream wastewater capacity rather than relying solely on traditional IEC 61131-compliant controller logic.
- **Four ICS Supply Chain Collaborative Outcomes**: Securing critical infrastructure requires collaboration across the entire lifecycle:
  1. *Secure Products*: Incorporating secure boot, root of trust, vulnerability identification pre-commercialization, secure update mechanisms, and communication drivers that uniquely identify endpoints, sign messages for integrity, and handle encryption.
  2. *Secure Deployment*: Hardening architectures through secure-by-design guidelines rather than relying on component-level security in isolation.
  3. *Continuous Health and Monitoring*: Implementing telemetry and collection management frameworks across deployed environments.
  4. *Incident Response*: Coordinating fast, structured defensive action across suppliers, integrators, and operators.
- **Gateway Threat Modeling & Hardware Trust**: The speaker describes collaborating with a third-party gateway supplier on a joint STRIDE-style threat model (analyzing spoofing, tampering, repudiation, denial of service, and information disclosure). This collaboration surfaced new hardware entropy sources, enforced port-level authentication, and implemented an automated self-provisioning manufacturing flow using certificate signing requests (CSRs) and API keys tied to an IoT shadow configuration.

### Takeaways
- Merely exchanging data or mandating compliance checklists like security questionnaires does not protect systems; questionnaires are expensive and easily bypassed.
- Effective defense requires establishing shared responsibility between asset owners/operators, integrators, and component manufacturers.
- Suppliers must provide greater visibility, understanding, and control, while operators must define concrete operational outcomes rather than relying on rigid, purely formal information channels.

talks.title: Attacks From The 4G/5G Core
talks.teaser: Discusses attacks From The 4G/5G Core and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how an attacker could reach a private cellular campus network and disrupt the industrial control system behind it. It explains private APNs in 4G and non-public networks in 5G across several deployment models. It also notes that standalone 5G moves core functions onto commercial servers and containers, adding exposure through out-of-band management cards, Kubernetes, Docker and routers.

The team built a small 4G lab with a small cell, an industrial router, a firewall, a historian, HMIs, an MQTT broker and PLCs. The base station itself exposed its IPsec pre-shared key to an unauthenticated user and let that user disable IPsec. Using netfilter queue, Scapy and iptables, they performed in-transit man-in-the-middle attacks: redirecting DNS answers to a rogue site, lowering a temperature value sent over MQTT by 20 degrees, and logging keystrokes from an unencrypted VNC session. In a simulated steel mill, altered data on the control HMI and the field HMI let operators see normal readings while the PLC behaved differently. Other demos covered unlimited password guessing via SMS on a Sierra Wireless router, PLC logic reset, and pass-the-hash.

The recommendations are to encrypt traffic with a VPN, IPsec or application-layer security rather than relying on the carrier or integrator, to patch every 5G component including servers and remote management cards, and to run anomaly detection across the campus network. Teams should also understand how the carrier slices and routes private APN traffic. In the Q&A, the speaker said the purchaser owns the campus network unless it is contracted out.

talks.title: CSAF, Not SBOM, Is The Solution
talks.teaser: Provides CSAF, Not SBOM, Is The Solution and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
This talk examines why acting on security advisories is so hard for operators of critical infrastructure. Operators prioritise uptime and revenue over cyber security, and each vulnerability forces a choice between patching now, patching at the next maintenance window, or accepting the risk. Advisories arrive as PDFs, HTML, text files, portal entries or emails, and the volume multiplied by installed devices makes manual tracking unrealistic. CVSS scores alone also ignore where a risk sits in a given installation.

The speaker proposes CSAF (Common Security Advisory Framework), an OASIS standard that defines the contents and mandatory fields of advisories in a machine-readable JSON format, which issuers can sign. Its product tree lets operators match advisories against their asset inventory. The speaker argues that an SBOM helps vendors with transparency but does not tell an operator whether they are affected or what to do. VEX, which is effectively a CSAF profile, lets vendors state whether a product is affected, not affected or still under investigation.

For vendors, the workflow means generating advisories from a content management system and signing them, with a converter or simple script for smaller companies. For operators, matching advisories to asset databases still needs manual work, and decision trees such as SSVC can help with triage. The speaker closes by urging vendors to publish in a structured format, noting that CSAF is being considered for the EU NIS2 discussions and that more vendors and tooling are on the way.
